Learning Objectives
Explain essential tensionless wound closure to minimize wound complications, including
infection.
Describe the phases of wound healing.
Review the current options for wound closure after orthopaedic surgery.
Apply the appropriate strategies for postoperative wound management and dressing care.
Introduction

Introduction
The primary objectives of wound closure after orthopaedic surgery are to ensure rapid
healing; avoid complications, including surgical site infection; and optimize the cosmetic

result for the patient. Properly performed tensionless wound closure is one of the most
important measures of protection against surgical site infection. Improper closure
technique may lead to early wound dehiscence, which is associated with higher rates of
surgical site infection.
Assessing the patient preoperatively and classifying the surgical wound as clean or
contaminated is crucial because this will inform the wound closure strategy and the
suture material (braided or nonbraided) that should be used. The location and depth of
the wound also must be considered. Preventing dead space by performing a layered
closure will prevent seroma or hematoma formation and help avoid infection.
Wound Classification
Clean: most planned surgical incisions 
Clean-contaminated: surgical wounds that may become contaminated 
Contaminated: open, traumatic wounds or infected surgical wounds 

Wound Classification
Wound contamination must be evaluated before determining wound closure strategy
because it will influence the type of closure and the type of suture material used.
Wounds may be clean, clean-contaminated, or contaminated. Most primary surgical
wounds in orthopaedics are considered clean (Figure 1). Clean wounds are intentional
incisions created during a surgical procedure performed under sterile conditions. If a
break in sterility occurs during a surgical procedure or contamination of a wound occurs
during a surgical procedure, such as perforation of the gastrointestinal tract, then the
wound is considered clean-contaminated. Open fractures and infected surgical incisions
are considered contaminated (Figure 2). Braided and nonabsorbable sutures should be
avoided in contaminated wounds.

Pathophysiology
Types of Wound Healing

The type of wound healing used is determined via classification of the wound.
Primary intention: most acute, clean surgical wounds that are manually reapproximated via
sutures, staples, or adhesive material (Figure 2).
Secondary intention: wounds allowed to heal via granulation and re-epithelialization; used
for certain contaminated wounds (Figure 3).
Tertiary Intention: if primary closure is delayed; allows the wound to granulate for a short
period before closure via manual reapproximation (delayed primary closure).
Figure 3 Clinical photographs of the proximal aspect of a surgical incision. A, Wound dehiscence
occurred. B, After several weeks of management via local wound care, the wound healed via
secondary intention.
Phases of Wound Healing
The inflammatory phase consists of the first 24 to 48 hours after an injury beginning with
hemostasis. Platelet aggregation forms the initial thrombus and releases growth factors that
recruit neutrophils and macrophages to the wound. The macrophages and neutrophils
remove necrotic tissue and bacteria, releasing cytokines. The wound, which starts as a
relatively acellular area, becomes cellular. Mast cells that release histamine also are recruited,
inducing redness, swelling, and pain.

The proliferative phase is initiated with the recruitment of fibroblasts to the wound, which
produce collagen and give the initial structure of wound healing. Epidermal cells begin to
proliferate and migrate until an epithelial bridge is formed.
The remodeling phase begins 2 to 3 weeks postinjury and occurs if the collagen is synthesized
at the same rate at which it is degraded.
Impaired Wound Healing
TIME Concept of Poor Wound Healing
An international group of wound healing experts developed the TIME framework to describe
the key elements of poor wound healing and to provide a more systematic approach to the
management of such wounds. 
Devitalized tissue (T) Devitalized tissue, including exudate, debris; and any non-viable tissue,
including host necrotic tissue, must be débrided. This can be done via mechanical
débridement, wet-to-dry dressing changes, or negative-pressure dressings. 
Inflammation or infection (I) Underlying infection must be addressed via anti-sepsis. Local
antibiotic or antiseptic management as well as systemic antibiosis may be used on a patient-
by-patient basis. 
Moisture imbalance (M) Excessive moisture is limited via débridement and/or dressing
changes. The amount of drainage or exudate also will determine the type and frequency of
dressing changes. 
Non-advancing wound edges (E) The size of the wound and the rate of contraction are major
considerations in wound management. For wounds that do not contract, split-thickness skin
grafting or muscle flap coverage may be considered.


Factors Affecting Wound Healing
Several factors, some of which are modifiable, may affect wound healing. Systemic
factors include diabetes mellitus, smoking, obesity, malnutrition, patient age, and
medications. Diabetes mellitus impairs wound healing via multiple pathways. Patients
with diabetes mellitus have decreased tissue perfusion and decreased angiogenesis,
which may lead to wound hypoxia and delayed wound healing. Patients with diabetes
mellitus also experience a decrease in the normal immune response, leading to a higher
risk of infection.2 Smoking and other forms of tobacco use are associated with wound
ischemia, which may lead to delayed wound healing and infection. Surgeons may
advocate delaying surgical procedure until a patient can cease smoking or until diabetes
mellitus control improves.3 Obesity also may delay wound healing via impaired tissue
oxygenation and impaired immune response. Direct tissue compromise may result from
overlying tissue in certain patients with obesity. Malnourished patients, including those
with obesity and poor nutrition, are at risk for impaired wound healing because they
have deficiencies in proteins that are essential for repairing wounds. In addition, every
phase of the healing process is affected by aging. Delayed T-cell infiltration to the wound,
delayed epithelialization, delayed angiogenesis, and diminished collagen turnover are
noted with advanced patient age.4 Similarly, ongoing steroid use or chemotherapy may
impair the immune response and delay wound healing. 
Skin thickness, skin integrity, and proximity to high bacterial burden are local factors
that may lead to problematic wound healing. For example, the incision for direct anterior
total hip arthroplasty is at risk for delayed or impaired healing in a patient with obesity
because the pannus may drape over the incision and limit circulation and hygiene to the
area.5 Wounds in a region of prior or ongoing radiation therapy also are at risk for
delayed healing secondary to impaired cell turnover and fibrosis of region.6


Skin Closure Techniques and Options
Selection of suture material, needle, and suturing techniques and configurations is
essential because no two wounds are the same. In selecting suture material and
configuration, surgeons must consider the type of wound (clean versus contaminated).
The technique selected for closure after orthopaedic surgery also varies depending on
anatomic area, type of surgical procedure, and surgeon preference. The adequacy of
blood flow to an area is highly associated with subsequent risk of infection and must be
considered in selecting the closure technique and materials. The size and depth of the
wound must be considered, and surgeons should evaluate for potential dead space
formation. Especially in larger patients, a dead space may allow for hematoma or
seroma formation that may serve as a nidus for infection or result in increasing wound
tension and lead to complications. Addressing dead space by closing the wound in layers
may be an important preventive measure. Incisions around joints also require special
consideration because tension around these areas is higher.

Barbed suture is more commonly used to close the fascia and the arthrotomy in total hip
arthroplasty and total knee arthroplasty, respectively. Studies have demonstrated that
barbed suture decreases closure time in arthroplasty.8,9
Braided or nonabsorbable suture generally is avoided in patients with a contaminated
wound because evidence shows that such sutures harbor more bacteria and retain more
biofilm than monofilament sutures.10
Suture size also varies based on to the tissue being closed. The larger the number, the
smaller the diameter of the suture material. Therefore, 0-Vicryl suture or larger typically is
used for deeper layers, whereas 2-0 Vicryl and 3-0 Vicryl sutures are used for more
superficial layers. 
Needle Selection
Shape 
Cutting versus tapered 

Needle Selection
Most needles are shaped with a 3/8 circle; however, a 1/2 circle needle may be helpful
for deeper wounds. The point of the needle is the most common variation that the
surgeon will be asked to select intraoperatively. Cutting and tapered needle points exist.
A cutting needle has three cutting edges that facilitate skin penetration. A tapered
needle has a round body that facilitates the spread of tissue. Tapered needles may be

are advantageous for closing skin edges.
Suture Configurations
Simple interrupted throws may facilitate skin edge approximation in most wounds.
Vertical and horizontal mattress sutures alleviate tension from the incision line itself and
promote skin edge eversion (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustration shows the horizontal mattress suture technique.

Suture Configurations
Fascia layers typically are closed via simple, interrupted throws of suture or a running
stitch with a regular or a barbed suture. Deeper layers in orthopaedic procedures

frequently can be closed via superficial to deep throws of sutures that facilitate wound
approximation while allowing for buried knots. Much variation exists with regard to
suture configuration options for the skin layer, depending on the wound.
Allgöwer-Donati Technique
Maintains the most cutaneous blood flow and is useful in high-risk incisions, such as calcaneus
fractures (Figure 5 and Figure 6)
Figure 5 Illustration shows the Allgöwer-Donati suture technique, which results in a knot applied
to one side of the incision and limits trauma to the wound edges. The knot is strategically placed
on the less tenuous side of the incision.

Staples
Avantages of staples include efficiency and a lower incidence of skin reaction. 
Disadvantages of staples include potentially poorer cosmesis and that they must be removed. 

Staples
Staples are advantageous because they are efficient and decrease the risk of needle-
stick injuries. Most staples are made of stainless steel and cause little skin reaction in
most patients. Staples may be associated with poorer cosmesistic because they leave
tracks around the skin edges. In addition, staple removal and may be painful.

Conflicting evidence exists with regard to the association between surgical site
infection and the use of staples versus sutures.11
Adhesives
2-octyl cyanoacrylate is a commonly used adhesive for wound or surgical incision closure. It
provides a seal to wounds and is associated with a decreased risk of surgical site infection.
Studies have demonstrated lower rates of wound drainage and surgical site infection after
arthroplasty and spine surgery with 2-octyl cyanoacrylate and staples compared with staples
alone.12,13
Polyester mesh has been used in combination with 2-octyl cyanoacrylate adhesive to decrease
tension over a surgical incision.14
Associated with 0.5% rate of allergic reaction, which may require management15 (Figure 7).
Figure 7 Intraoperative photograph of the hip of a patient after revision total hip arthroplasty
shows polyester mesh applied to the skin after closure with the use of a 3-0 Monocryl running
suture. (Courtesy of Elizabeth B. Gausden, MD, MPH, New York, NY.)
Types of Dressings
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:54 PM
AAOS | Principles of Wound Closure
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002117
12/17

Films
Films are simple dressings that have adhesives to keep the dressing attached and prevent
contamination of the wound.
Enhanced dressings
A silver-impregnated, occlusive hydrofiber-based dressing is designed to cover a surgical
wound for the first 7 days.
A silicone dressing has been associated with lower rates of blister formation.
Negative pressure wound therapy promotes wound healing via various mechanisms.16,17
Subatmospheric pressure is applied to a wound via a sealed dressing that is connected to
suction and a drainage collection system.
The effect of the negative pressure in a sealed environment is increased blood flow and the
stimulation of angiogenesis. This leads to increased granulation tissue formation, decreased
wound surface area, and lower rate of seroma formation.18
The sealed environment and negative pressure lower the bacterial burden of contaminated
wounds. Therefore, negative pressure dressings are useful for high-risk clean surgical
wounds and in patients at risk for surgical site infection.19

Types of Dressings
The ideal postoperative dressing protects tissues from stress, prevents contamination
from exterior sources, and prevents cellular dehydration.16 Dressings coated with
antimicrobial and antiseptic agents are increasingly being used in orthopaedics to
decrease bacterial growth around surgical wounds (Video 1).

Summary

Summary
Adhering to principles of wound closure in orthopaedic surgery may help surgeons avoid
unnecessary wound healing problems and surgical site infections. Each wound should be
analyzed individually with regard to the type of wound, patient risk factors for wound
healing problems, the location of the wound, and the size/depth of the wound. Use of
the appropriate type of wound closure, suture material, technique, and wound dressing
is essential to successful wound management.
